eps.d: The inaugural edition of 'Tomorrow's World' presents a report on the state of the art in kidney dialysis machines capable of being used in the patient's home; A report on lessons in fresh water management drawn from the Dutch flood defence system; and a look at the possibility that the Mariner 4 space probe may uncover evidence of life on Mars.
Tomorrow's World broadcasts live from an operating theatre where a patient is undergoing laser eye surgery.

eps.t: A Tomorrow's World Special from Alaska
eps.d: First transmitted in 1969, James Burke reports on America's attempts to turn Alaska in a 'gold mine' for the second time since gold was first discovered in the late 1890s.
Derek Cooper introduces the Moog synthesiser, an instrument that can produce a variety of noises and arrangements, both mimicking real instruments and creating new sounds, all electronically.
Programme exploring current trends in science and future developments. Derek Cooper reports on developments in computers that could revolutionise banking.

Christmas special of the science magazine programme from 1975. Raymond Baxter, William Woollard, Michael Rodd and Judith Hann invite a party of children to their workshop, where young and old can enjoy magic moments of science.
In the last edition of the 1970s, the team reviews and updates a selection of past reports. Items include the progress of the Channel Tunnel.

As 'Tomorrow's World' goes off the air for a summer break, the series concludes with a timely look back at some items from the past year. Michael Rodd simplifies solar physics and studies otters in a California zoo, while Kieran Prendiville road-tests a new timber tractor.
The current Tomorrow's World team is joined by some of the original presenters to highlight various developments that have become fundamental to our way of life.

Technology-based yuletide shenanigans from the Stableford/Hann/MacCann-era Tomorrow's World (i.e. late 80s). We can't remember much about this, though there was probably a "what happened next" archive round, and much "guess what this is for" jollity.
First transmitted in 1987, what is the future of manned space flight one year after the US Challenger disaster?

The first edition of 1988, presented by the classic line-up of Judith Hann, Maggie Philbin, Peter Macann and Howard Stableford. Futuristic features include an incredible LCD strip that can actually tell you how much power is left in a battery, a Telecine machine that can miraculously remove scratches from old film, and a very young looking Stephen Hawking showing off his amazing new computerized…

This week: the plane that is carried in the back of the car, and why Leningrad's collection of historic books were put into the city's deepfreeze. With Judith Hann, Howard Stableford, Peter Macann and Kate Bellingham.

The Rubik Cube made its Hungarian inventor Erno Rubik a millionaire, but he used the money wisely. With Judith Hann , Howard Stableford, Kate Bellingham and Peter Macann. Producer Cynthia Page Editor Dana Purvis

This week Bob Symes takes to the water and tries out a fishy idea. Also there's news of scientific research in Germany as east and west team up to improve artificial heart valves. With Judith Hann , Howard Stableford, Kate Bellingham and Peter Macann. Producer Cynthia Page Editor Dana Purvis

How Britain's threatened wetlands are being protected by bird watchers in space; and is there a future for the artificial heart? With Judith Hann , Howard Stableford,Peter Macann and Kate Bellingham. Producer Cynthia Page Editor Dana Purvis

This week: a vision of the future - how robots are learning to look at chocolates, cars and chips. And the sound of the future - can music sound larger than life? Viewers have their own opportunity to sample 3-D stereo by tuning in to a live link-up with Radio l's Mark Goodier 's Evening Session. With Judith Hann , Howard Stableford, Kate Bellingham and Peter Macann.
A look at recent technological developments. In this programme, the team look at geothermal energy, shock absorbers and heat resistant gel.

eps.t: The End of the Cold War Space Race
eps.d: Tomorrow's World Tonight's special edition marks the end of the cold war space race and the beginning of a new era of space exploration. With Howard Stableford, Shahnaz Pakravan and Sam Roberts.
First transmitted in 1995, this special edition marks the end of the cold war space race and the beginning of a new era of space exploration.

In a programme from 1997, a look at how pigs' hearts are being used in human transplants; tests for potentially lethal genetic defects; how body odours attract the opposite sex; and how DNA traces could identify the genes that can be used in facial reconstruction.

Peter Snow and Lindsey Fallow present a special edition of Tomorrow's World, live from the BBC Futureworld exhibition in Bristol - which aims to showcase the future of digital broadcasting, television and the internet. In this edition, Anya Sitaram reports on digital avatars, and meets her own digital clone.

A special programme live from Cornwall's Eden Project, the largest greenhouse in the world, which investigates whether fear of heights could be cured through virtual reality. The first woman to receive this pioneering treatment attempts a terrifying abseil off the top of a dome. There is also a report on how psychometric testing could find families the perfect pet.

Tonight, a look at the scientific facts behind this summer's Spider-Man movie. Including exclusive access to the new technology used in bringing the superhero to the big screen, plus interviews with the director Sam Raimi, and stars, Willem Defoe, Tobey Maguire and Kirsten Dunst.
